name: Kharam Naga
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress
sweep_summary: Kharam Naga (khar1288) is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword hit in the sweep list (Christou & Baltazani 2010, stressed vowels in the Greek dialect of Kato Pedina) is a Glottolog computational mis-assignment ('kato and the'), concerns Modern Greek, and is irrelevant; not fetched sources. The only first-hand description of Kharam, Singh 2014 (Assam University PhD, on file from the earlier pass at, treats the language as tonal (two lexical tones, high/low, ch. III p. 12-14) and contains no statement on word stress or accent (zero hits for stress/accent across all chapters). Haokip 2011 (LTBA) has no phonology for Kharam. Additional bibliographic searches this sweep (Crossref title search: no linguistic hits; OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar: rate-limited; OLAC: unreachable; No word-stress statement exists to record; nothing to acquire. Sweep note appended to

sources.citation: Singh, Khaidem Dutta (2014). A Descriptive Study of Kharam: An Endangered Language of Northeastern India. PhD thesis, Assam University, Silchar. 243 pp.
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.quote: Like the majority of Sino-Tibetan languages, Kharam is a tonal language in which a change in the pitch of the syllable corresponds to a change in its meaning. Kharam has two contrastive lexical tones: high and low. However the analysis of tones is not extensive in this present study and the further research is required to draw the exhaustive tonal structure of the language.
sources.locator: ch. III Phonology, sec. 3.1 p. 12 and sec. 3.2 'Tones' p. 14
sources.note: The only phonological description of Kharam. Ch. III sec. 3.1 (p. 12) lists two suprasegmental phonemes, both tones; sec. 3.2 (p. 14) describes two contrastive lexical tones (high/low) with minimal pairs pa 'father'/'mushroom', tu 'who'/'feed'. A grep of every chapter text for 'stress' and 'accent' returns zero hits; the thesis makes no statement about word-stress placement. Silent on stress; describes the language as tonal.
